sections.text:
After the great flood, the descendants of those who survived with Noah, peace be upon him, multiplied and populated the earth again.

Among these was the Aad tribe, which inhabited the Al-Ahqaf region in the south of the Arabian Peninsula.

The people of Aad had tremendous physical strength. They were tall, massive, and powerful like no other.

Thanks to their power, they built a great civilization and luxurious cities, the most prominent of which is the city of “Iram the Pillar,” the likes of which had never been created in the country.

They built luxurious palaces and tents raised with huge columns, and carved houses and factories in the mountains, thinking that they were immortal.

God blessed them with fertile lands, abundant water springs, and countless livestock and orchards.

But instead of thanking God for these great blessings, they became arrogant and arrogant, and were deceived by their physical and material strength.

They said with all arrogance and arrogance: “Who is stronger than us?” And they forgot that God, who created them, is stronger than them.

They deviated from the worship of God, and carved idols of stones (Sada, Samud, and Vaha) and began to worship them and offer sacrifices to them.

In order for God to return them to the path of truth, He sent to them a man from among them, the Prophet Hud, peace be upon him.

Hud was a wise and righteous man. He stood among them and said with a loving heart: “O my people, worship God. You have no god but Him.”

He reminded them of God’s grace upon them, and how He made them caliphs on earth after Noah’s people, and how He increased them in creation and power.

He called on them to seek forgiveness and repent, and promised them that God would increase their strength and send rain upon them if they believed.

But the people of Ad responded to him with ridicule and ridicule, accusing him of foolishness, lying, and that the gods had made him mad.

They said to him: “You have not brought us any proof, and we are not abandoning our gods based on your words, and we are not believers in you.”

Hood challenged them with courage and confidence in God, and told them that he relied on God, in whose hand are the forelocks of all animals.

Hood continued to invite him for a long time, but they insisted on their stubbornness and challenged him, saying: “Then bring us what you promise us if you are of the truthful ones.”

God's wrath was upon the people of Aad for their persistence in disbelief and tyranny, and torment began to gradually descend upon them.

God withheld rain from them for years, so their lands became drought-stricken, their crops perished, and their livestock died of thirst.

They were looking at the sky desperately waiting for rain, and one day, they saw a huge black cloud heading towards them.

They were happy and danced, thinking that it was a cloud carrying heavy rain, and they said happily: “This is a rainy season for us.”

But Hud said to them sadly, warning: “Rather, it is what you have been hasty in. It is a smell in which there is a painful punishment.”

The wind began to blow. It was not just an ordinary wind, but rather a “strong cricket wind,” extremely cold, strong, and fast.

God gave them control over seven nights and eight days, continuously and without interruption.

The wind was strong, uprooting trees from their roots, and demolishing luxurious palaces on the heads of their owners.

She would lift the huge man high into the air and then throw him to the ground, breaking his neck and separating his head from his body.

They became as if they were empty palm leaves, lying on the ground, and all that could be seen was their destroyed homes, which were a symbol of their power.

The entire tribe of Ad perished, but God saved Hud and those who believed with him through His mercy.

The moral of Hood's story is that material power and urban development are of no use if faith and morals are absent.

Vanity and arrogance are among the most dangerous diseases that destroy nations and civilizations, no matter how great they are.
